core.text: Deponents give orders with **the deponent command forms (sequere! = follow!, sequimini! = follow, all of you!)**. To one person the command ends in -re: *sequere!* (follow!), *laetāre!* (rejoice!), *intuēre!* (look!). To several it ends in -minī: *sequiminī!*, *laetāminī!*, *intuēminī!* — the same as the passive 'you all' ending. Latin name: *imperātīvus verbōrum dēpōnentium*.
A command in English is the bare verb: *follow me!* Latin needs the right ending for one listener or many.
Singular: present stem + -re (laetāre, intuēre, sequere, partīre). Plural: present stem + -minī (laetāminī, intuēminī, sequiminī, partīminī).

*Sequere* looks like the active infinitive (the 'to' form) of a third-conjugation verb (*legere*), but *sequī* is deponent — its infinitive is *sequī* — so *sequere* can only be a command. Rule of thumb: if the dictionary form ends in -ī, a form in -re is 'do it!', not 'to do'.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 25 review) put it as: the deponent infinitive-lookalike is the singular command (*intuērī → intuēre*, *cōnsōlārī → cōnsōlāre*, *cōnfitērī → cōnfitēre*), the plural uses -minī (*intuēminī, sequiminī, laetāminī*).

Ørberg (cap. XXV) lines them up against active commands: *laetāre! = gaudē!*, *intuēre! = spectā!*, *revertere! = redī!*, *partīre! = dīvide!*. For 'don't', use *nōlī / nōlīte* + deponent infinitive: *nōlī mīrārī!*

teach.title: Ordering someone about with a deponent
teach.say: A deponent (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) gives its orders with **the deponent command forms (sequere! = follow!, sequiminī! = follow, all of you!)**. *Sequere mē, Mārce, in hortum!* — one word, one order, exactly as blunt as the English 'Follow me!'

teach.title: To one person: -re
teach.say: Speaking to one person, add *-re* to the present stem with the verb's own linking vowel in front: long *ā* in the first conjugation (*laetā-re*), long *ē* in the second (*intuē-re*), short *e* in the third (*sequ-e-re*), long *ī* in the fourth (*partī-re*).

show.say: sequere — the stem sequ-, the linking -e-, then -re

teach.title: To several: -minī
teach.say: Speaking to more than one, the ending is *-minī*, with that same linking vowel in front: *laetā-minī*, *intuē-minī*, *sequ-i-minī*, *partī-minī*. It is the same *-minī* that means 'you all' in the passive, and it never varies. Beside an ordinary verb's *-te* it looks quite different: *Vidēte … et intuēminī!*

show.say: sequiminī — the stem sequ-, the linking -i-, then -minī

teach.title: Why -re here is not 'to do'
teach.say: *Legere* means 'to read'; *sequere* means 'follow!'. They rhyme because the deponent has borrowed the passive's shape. The dictionary settles it: *legō, legere* is an ordinary verb, so its *-re* form is the infinitive (the 'to' form); *sequor, sequī* is a deponent whose infinitive is *sequī*, so *sequere* can only be an order.

teach.title: Saying 'don't'
teach.say: For a negative order these forms are not used at all. Latin puts *nōlī* (to one person) or *nōlīte* (to several) in front of the deponent's infinitive: *Nōlī sequī Mēdum!* — don't follow Medus; *Nōlīte proficīscī!* — don't set out. The half of the order that says what to do keeps its own *-re* or *-minī* form: *sed mē sequere!*
